title: The Poster and the Epic: a Moravian in Paris, and the Twenty Canvases He Went Home to Paint
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Ivancice, the court usher's son
stops.date_confidence: attested; the birthplace pin is the town square of Ivancice, corrected from a coordinate in the research pool that fell some six hundred metres south of the town
stops.campa: In the market town of Ivancice, in Moravia under the Austrian Empire, a court usher's wife bears a son on the twenty-fourth of July and the family names him Alfons Maria. His father copies documents for the district court all his working life; his mother had been a governess. The boy draws before he writes, and the parish keeps a Crucifixion he makes at eight, a child's drawing already arranged like an altarpiece, the figure set inside a frame of ornament. Nothing in the household suggests Paris.
suggested_refs: The Mucha birth house on Palackeho namesti, Ivancice
The childhood Crucifixion drawing, c. 1868, Mucha Foundation collection

stops.name: Brno, the choral scholarship
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1872 by the Mucha Foundation timeline; a widespread biographical tradition dates the Brno choir years to 1870 and makes Leos Janacek the choirmaster, which the Wikipedia account contradicts
stops.campa: A choral scholarship carries him to the Slavonic Gymnasium in Brno, where he sings in the choir of the church of Saints Peter and Paul and lives inside the sound of the Mass. The choirmaster, Pavel Krizkovsky, is impressed by the boy and cannot fund him: he has just taken in another gifted young musician, Leos Janacek, who sings beside him. Mucha stays in the choir anyway, singing the daily offices under the vaults of Saints Peter and Paul, and learns the plainchant and the ornament on the walls of that church in the same years and in the same room.
stops.quote: For me, the notions of painting, going to church, and music are so closely knit that often I cannot decide whether I like church for its music, or music for its place in the mystery which it accompanies.
stops.quote_source: Mucha, quoted in Tomoko Sato, Mucha (Taschen, 2015), p. 9, as cited on the English Wikipedia article
suggested_refs: The Cathedral of Saints Peter and Paul, Brno, and its choir registers
Gymnazium Slovanske, Brno, scholarship records

stops.name: Prague, the Academy says no
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1878; the advice to find another career is reported rather than documented, and the pin is the canonical Prague centre rather than the Academy's 1878 premises, which the sources consulted do not locate
stops.campa: He submits his drawings to the Academy of Fine Arts in Prague and is turned down, reportedly advised to look for a different line of work. He is eighteen, with no training beyond a provincial gymnasium and a parish choir loft. The rejection is never appealed and never rescinded. He goes back to Ivancice and takes a clerk's post in the district court, the office his father works in, copying documents in a good hand at the rate the court sets, and two years pass that way.
suggested_refs: Academy of Fine Arts in Prague, admissions records for 1878

stops.name: Vienna, the scenery workshop
stops.date_confidence: attested; he is nineteen on arrival and the firm's name is given variously as Kautsky-Brioschi-Burghart and Kautsky-Brioschi-Burghardt
stops.campa: At nineteen he answers an advertisement and is taken on as an apprentice scenery painter by Kautsky, Brioschi and Burghart, the firm that dresses the stages of imperial Vienna. He grinds pigment, squares up cartoons, and paints backdrops by the acre, learning the trade at the scale a theatre demands: a face that must read from forty rows back, a garden that must hold under gaslight. Evenings he draws in the galleries at his own expense. It is the only training in painting he has for the next six years.
suggested_refs: Surviving Kautsky-Brioschi-Burghart stage designs, Theatermuseum Vienna

stops.name: Vienna, the Ringtheater burns
stops.date_confidence: attested for the fire; the causal link to Mucha's dismissal is the standard biographical account rather than a documented employment record
stops.campa: On the eighth of December the Ring Theatre burns during a performance of Offenbach's Tales of Hoffmann and close to four hundred people die in the stairwells and the dark. The house is the workshop's largest client. Gas battens, painted flats, varnished canvas: everything the firm supplies is what carries the fire. Work stops, and the youngest hands go first. Mucha is twenty-one. He leaves Vienna with a few gulden and a portfolio of stage cartoons.
suggested_refs: The Ringtheater fire of 8 December 1881 and the Suehnhaus built on the site

stops.name: Mikulov, painting for whoever pays
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia dates the move to Mikulov to 1881, the same year as the December fire that is given as its cause; the sources do not resolve the order and the strain is left standing
stops.campa: He settles in Mikulov in southern Moravia and lives by his hands: portraits of the town's families, decorative panels, lettered signs, inscriptions cut for headstones, whatever is asked for. A local showing of the portraits makes his name across the district within a season. He is a jobbing painter with no school behind him, working under the Palava hills, and the work is good enough that word of it travels to a castle in the woods where a count wants a dining room painted.
suggested_refs: Mikulov portrait commissions of 1881-1882, Regional Museum Mikulov

stops.name: Sanov, the murals at Emmahof
stops.date_confidence: the Mucha Foundation timeline dates the first Emmahof commission to 1882 and the general chronology to 1883; the site is Emin zamek in the woods of Sanov, four kilometres west of Hrusovany nad Jevisovkou, not the Hrusovany near Brno given in the research pool
stops.campa: Count Khuen Belasi hires him to paint the dining room of Emmahof, a house standing in forest on the Jevisovka, and Mucha covers walls and ceiling with allegories he invents as he goes. The count's library is open to him, and so is the count's collection of engravings. It is the first work he does for a patron rather than a customer, and Mucha is twenty-two and has never been inside an academy. Watching the walls fill week by week, Belasi decides the young man should be trained properly and offers to send him to Munich at his own expense.
suggested_refs: Emin zamek (Emmahof), Sanov, Znojmo district, and its surviving Mucha decoration

stops.name: Eppan, the Tyrolean seat
stops.date_confidence: attested that the commission extended to Gandegg; the coordinates are corrected to Schloss Gandegg in the Pigeno district of Eppan, some thirteen kilometres from the pin supplied in the research pool
stops.campa: The commission follows the family south over the Alps to Gandegg, the Belasi seat above Eppan in the South Tyrol, and Mucha paints there through part of the mid-eighteen-eighties among vineyards and Italian light. He is kept as a member of the household rather than as a tradesman, travels with it, and paints its relatives. These are the last years of his life without a plan for it. When the scaffolding comes down he is sent to Munich with the count paying the fees.
suggested_refs: Schloss Gandegg, Eppan an der Weinstrasse, South Tyrol

stops.name: Munich, the student at twenty-five
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1885
stops.campa: With Belasi's money he enrols at the Academy of Fine Arts in Munich, twenty-five years old and finally a student. He works from the model and from plaster and learns the German academic drawing that will sit underneath every ornamental line he draws later. He falls in with the Czech and Slavic contingent and is elected chairman of the Skreta Group, named for the Bohemian painter of the seventeenth century. The group meets, argues, and writes home.
stops.quote: Here I am in my new element, painting. I cross all sorts of currents, but without effort, and even with joy. Here, for the first time, I can find the objectives to reach which used to seem inaccessible.
stops.quote_source: Mucha on Munich, quoted in Philippe Thiebaut, Mucha et l'Art Nouveau (2018), p. 22, as cited on the English Wikipedia article
suggested_refs: Academy of Fine Arts Munich, matriculation register 1885
Records of the Skreta Group of Slavic students

stops.name: Munich, the altarpiece for a prairie parish
stops.date_confidence: the commission is attested; no source places Mucha in North Dakota, and the picture is understood to have been painted in Europe and shipped
stops.campa: A Czech immigrant parish on the prairie of North Dakota, at a settlement its founders have named Pisek after the town in Bohemia, wants an altar picture of Saints Cyril and Methodius, the brothers who brought the Slavs their letters. The commission reaches him through the Skreta Group's American connections. He paints it in Munich, and it is crated and shipped. He never sees the church, the prairie, or the congregation that prays under it. His first Slavic apostles cross the Atlantic eighteen years before he does.
suggested_refs: Saints Cyril and Methodius Church, Pisek, Walsh County, North Dakota, and its Mucha altarpiece

stops.name: Paris, the Academie Julian
stops.date_confidence: Belasi agrees to fund the Paris move in 1887 and the Julian enrolment is dated 1888
stops.campa: He arrives in Paris and enrols at the Academie Julian, twenty-seven years old and older than most of the men at the easels around him. The corrections are given by Jules Lefebvre, Gustave Boulanger, and Jean-Paul Laurens, and the studios are packed shoulder to shoulder with foreigners, nobody in them asking him where he is from. He takes lodgings at 1 rue Bara in the Latin Quarter and draws from the nude every morning of the week. The fees, the room, and the paper are all still being paid for out of the Belasi estates.
suggested_refs: Academie Julian enrolment registers, 1888
1 rue Bara, Paris, his first Latin Quarter address

stops.name: Paris, the subsidy ends at the Colarossi
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Colarossi address on the rue de la Grande-Chaumiere is documented from 1879 to the 1930s, so the dating is secure even where the exact month is not
stops.campa: He moves his enrolment to the Academie Colarossi on the rue de la Grande-Chaumiere, where women draw from the nude alongside men and the fees are lower. Within the year Khuen Belasi stops the subsidy. There is no quarrel on record; the money simply ends after seven years of it. Mucha is turning thirty and has to eat. He takes whatever illustration work Paris gives a foreigner with a good hand: magazine covers, story headpieces, calendar plates, anything paid for by the drawing.
suggested_refs: Academie Colarossi, 10 rue de la Grande-Chaumiere, Paris

stops.name: Paris, Madame Charlotte's cremerie
stops.date_confidence: the Maupassant cover in La Vie populaire is dated 22 May 1890; the cremerie years are attested more loosely as around 1890
stops.campa: He becomes a fixture at Madame Charlotte's cremerie a few doors along, where the proprietress feeds hungry artists on credit and the tables run to half the Nordic colony of Montparnasse. On the twenty-second of May his illustration for a story by Guy de Maupassant runs on the cover of La Vie populaire. This is the whole of his living: sheets of paper, priced by the sheet, delivered on time. A Franco-Prussian war scene of his fills the cover of Le Petit Francais illustre on the twenty-third of January 1892.
suggested_refs: La Vie populaire, 22 May 1890, cover illustration
Le Petit Francais illustre, 23 January 1892

stops.name: Paris, the studio shared with Gauguin
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia dates the shared studio to Gauguin's return from Tahiti in the summer of 1893 and the Strindberg friendship to late autumn 1894; a line in the research pool dating both to 1890 is contradicted by the same pool's geography and is not followed here
stops.campa: Gauguin comes back from Tahiti in the summer with nowhere to work, and the two of them share the studio on the rue de la Grande-Chaumiere, the Tahitian canvases stacked against the wall of a room where Mucha is drawing calendar plates to pay the rent. Here he buys his first camera and starts photographing his models, and himself, posed in the exact attitudes he means to draw. In the late autumn of the following year he falls in with August Strindberg, and they sit up over the occult together.
suggested_refs: Mucha's studio photographs of models and of himself, 1893-1900, Mucha Foundation
The photograph of Gauguin at the harmonium in Mucha's studio

stops.name: Paris, Bernhardt sends for a poster
stops.date_confidence: attested to 26 December 1894; the coordinates are the canonical atlas pin for the Theatre de la Renaissance, which differs by some two hundred metres from the coordinates supplied in the research pool
stops.campa: On the twenty-sixth of December, with the shop's regular artists away for the holidays, the printer Lemercier has no one to answer Sarah Bernhardt's demand for a new poster for the continuing run of Gismonda at the Theatre de la Renaissance. Mucha is in the shop correcting proofs and is handed the job. He goes to the theatre, watches her from the house, and draws her standing, life-size, narrow as a column, in the palm procession of the last act. Earlier that year four of his illustrations had taken a medal at the Salon.
suggested_refs: Lemercier printing house records, December 1894
Victorien Sardou, Gismonda, Theatre de la Renaissance, 1894-1895 run

stops.name: Paris, the poster on the walls
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1 January 1895; the pin is the canonical Paris coordinate used across the atlas for the Gismonda event
stops.campa: On New Year's Day the bill-stickers put it up across the city: a woman nearly two metres tall on a narrow strip of paper, a mosaic halo behind her head, pale colours where the trade shouts, and BERNHARDT lettered as though cut in Byzantium. Paris stops in front of it. Collectors bribe the bill-stickers to cut sheets down before the paste dries. Bernhardt orders four thousand more and puts the unknown Moravian under a six-year contract for her posters, her sets, and her costumes. Paul Berthon will be drawing her in this attitude six years later.
suggested_refs: Gismonda, colour lithograph, Paris 1895
Paul Berthon's Bernhardt lithographs of 1901, which take the Gismonda format as settled

stops.name: Paris, the studio on the rue du Val-de-Grace
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1896 for both the studio and The Seasons
stops.campa: Under contract to Bernhardt and to the printer Champenois, he takes a larger studio on the rue du Val-de-Grace and hires assistants. For Champenois he makes The Seasons, four panels in which the women are the year itself: spring with the branch, summer in the water, autumn among the fruit, winter closed into the snow. They are sold as decoration, printed by the thousand, and pinned up in rooms that will never own a painting. Champenois pays a monthly retainer and takes everything he draws.
suggested_refs: The Seasons, decorative panels for F. Champenois, 1896
Champenois contract ledgers

stops.name: Paris, four hundred and forty-eight works
stops.date_confidence: the 448-work retrospective at the Salon des Cent is 1897; a line in the research pool placing it in 1896 conflates it with his first invitation to that gallery
stops.campa: The Salon des Cent, the gallery of the review La Plume, hangs four hundred and forty-eight of his works, months after the smaller showing of a hundred and seven at the Galerie de la Bodiniere. The retrospective travels on to Vienna, Prague, Munich, Brussels, London, and New York. He is thirty-seven and the most reproduced draughtsman in Europe. Champenois cannot print the panels fast enough, dealers cut them from the hoardings, and imitators in four countries are drawing his women with his hair and his haloes.
stops.quote: I had not found any real satisfaction in my old kind of work. I saw that my way was to be found elsewhere, little bit higher.
stops.quote_source: Mucha, quoted in Philippe Thiebaut, Mucha et l'Art Nouveau (2018), p. 111, as cited on the English Wikipedia article
suggested_refs: Salon des Cent, 31 rue Bonaparte, exhibition catalogue 1897
Galerie de la Bodiniere, 18 rue Saint-Lazare, 1897 solo exhibition

stops.name: Paris, Le Pater in five hundred and ten copies
stops.date_confidence: attested to 20 December 1899; his admission to a lodge of the Grand Orient de France is dated January 1898
stops.campa: He designs, letters, and illustrates his own book: the Lord's Prayer broken into seven petitions, each given a page of symbolist ornament, a page of calligraphy, and a page of image, printed in five hundred and ten copies and published on the twentieth of December. He calls it the thing he has made that he most cares for. Two years earlier he had entered a lodge of the Grand Orient de France, and the book reads as a Mason's cosmology as much as a Christian one, mankind climbing out of darkness by stages.
stops.quote: First a cover page with symbolist ornament; then the same ornament developed in a kind a variation on each line of the prayer; a page explaining each line in a calligraphic form; and a page rendering the idea of each line in the form of an image.
stops.quote_source: Mucha describing the structure of Le Pater, quoted in Philippe Thiebaut, Mucha et l'Art Nouveau (2018), p. 111, as cited on the English Wikipedia article
suggested_refs: Le Pater, Paris 1899, edition of 510
Charles Masson's contemporary review of Le Pater, which calls Mucha a visionary

stops.name: Sarajevo, the Bascarsija sketchbooks
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1899 by the Mucha Foundation timeline as preparation for the 1900 pavilion
stops.campa: The Austrian government gives him the Bosnia and Herzegovina pavilion for the coming World's Fair, and he goes to the Balkans to look at what he is being asked to decorate. In Sarajevo he walks the Bascarsija, draws Ottoman metalwork and Slavic embroidery, listens to the songs in the coffee houses, and fills sketchbooks with a Slavdom he had only imagined from Montparnasse. Vienna wants a province shown pacified and picturesque. When he decides instead to tell the history of the southern Slavs through their defeats, the sketchbooks do not say.
suggested_refs: Mucha's Balkan sketchbooks of 1899, Mucha Foundation

stops.name: Paris, the pavilion on the Rue des Nations
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1900; the pavilion stood on the Rue des Nations along the Quai d'Orsay, not on the Champ de Mars as the research pool placed it
stops.campa: Along the Rue des Nations on the left bank, between the Pont des Invalides and the Pont de l'Alma, the pavilions of the nations stand in a row, and Karl Panek's Bosnian pavilion carries Mucha's murals of Slavic history round its walls. His own watercolours hang in the Austrian pavilion. He takes a silver medal, the Knight's cross of the Order of Franz Joseph from Vienna, and the Legion of Honour from France, decorated in the same season by the empire he is quietly painting against.
stops.quote: a Czech from Moravia not only by birth and origin, but also by feeling, by conviction and by patriotism
stops.quote_source: Sarah Bernhardt describing Mucha to the French public, quoted in Tomoko Sato, Mucha (Taschen, 2015), p. 46, as cited on the English Wikipedia article
suggested_refs: Bosnia-Herzegovina Pavilion, Exposition Universelle 1900, architect Karl Panek
The Austrian Pavilion watercolours of 1900

stops.name: Paris, the whole of a jeweller's shop
stops.date_confidence: the shop interior is completed in 1901 and dismantled in 1923; the serpent bracelet for Bernhardt is 1899, not 1900 as one line of the research pool has it
stops.campa: The jeweller Georges Fouquet, who two years before had a serpent bracelet made to Mucha's design for Bernhardt's hand, gives him the whole of his new shop at 6 rue Royale: the front, the cases, the stained glass, the peacock bronzes, the fountain, the furniture, one continuous ornament from door to ceiling. He goes on refusing the name the movement is being given. The next year he publishes Documents Decoratifs, seventy-two plates of his own line put at the disposal of other people's work, printed for the use of any manufacturer who buys the folio.
stops.quote: What is it, Art Nouveau? ...Art can never be new.
stops.quote_source: Mucha, reported by his son Jiri Mucha, quoted in Tomoko Sato, Mucha (Taschen, 2015), p. 43, as cited on the English Wikipedia article
suggested_refs: The Fouquet boutique interior, reassembled at the Musee Carnavalet, Paris
Documents Decoratifs, Paris 1902, 72 plates

stops.name: Prague, showing Rodin the country
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1902 by the Mucha Foundation timeline
stops.campa: He brings Auguste Rodin to Prague and then out into Moravia: the villages, the costumes, the country the posters never had anything to do with. The friendship was made in the Paris of the pavilions and the exhibitions, and now the most celebrated sculptor in Europe is walking through Mucha's birthplace behind him. Mucha is forty-two, at the top of a career he has begun describing as a detour, and showing a Frenchman the villages he was raised among. They are photographed among people in embroidered linen, two famous Parisians in city hats.
suggested_refs: Photographs of the Mucha and Rodin journey through Moravia, 1902
auguste_rodin.journey.json, Colegio Invisible atlas

stops.name: New York, the first crossing
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1904 as the first of five American trips, each of five or six months
stops.campa: He lands in New York in March, already famous there because Bernhardt has toured the country under his posters for a decade, and the newspapers meet the boat. He takes a studio near Central Park and sets himself up as a portraitist to the rich. It is the first of five crossings, each lasting five or six months over the next six years, and the purpose under all of them is money for a project no American has yet heard of. The society commissions come slowly and pay less than Champenois did.
suggested_refs: New York press coverage of Mucha's arrival, spring 1904

stops.name: New York, teaching the ornamental grammar
stops.date_confidence: attested that he taught at the New York School of Applied Design for Women and for five weeks in Philadelphia; the pin is the school's later Lexington Avenue building, which was not built until 1908, so the 1905 premises cannot be located from the sources consulted
stops.campa: He teaches at the New York School of Applied Design for Women, and for five weeks at the Philadelphia school, drilling students through the ornamental grammar he had printed as plates three years earlier: how a border turns a corner, how a head sits inside an arc. In every room he is introduced into he is looking for somebody with money and a feeling for Slavs. New York looks at him and sees the Bernhardt posters. The classes pay steadily; the portrait commissions do not.
suggested_refs: New York School of Applied Design for Women, 160 Lexington Avenue (occupied from 1909)
Documents Decoratifs as a teaching text in American design schools

stops.name: Prague, the marriage to Maruska
stops.date_confidence: attested to 10 June 1906
stops.campa: He marries Marie Chytilova, called Maruska, in Prague on the tenth of June. She is an art student twenty-two years younger, whom he met in Paris while she was studying there and he was teaching. He is forty-five and has lived alone in rented studios since he was nineteen. Within the year they sail for the United States together, and she will keep his household in New York, in Chicago, in the rented rooms at Zbiroh and in Prague, for the thirty-three years he has left. Their first child is born in Manhattan and their second in Prague.
suggested_refs: Marie Muchova-Chytilova, letters and household papers, Mucha Foundation

stops.name: Chicago, the visiting professor
stops.date_confidence: attested as a visiting professorship at the Art Institute of Chicago during trips of five or six months between 1906 and 1910; the research pool's phrasing that the couple relocated to Chicago overstates a pattern of repeat visits
stops.campa: He takes up a visiting professorship at the Art Institute of Chicago, teaching in the city with the largest Czech population outside Bohemia. The Czechs of Chicago and their newspapers know exactly who he is, and they come to hear him speak about Slav history rather than about ornament. Between the classes he is introduced to the men in that world who have money. He is a repeat visitor rather than a resident, five or six months at a stretch, with Marie travelling on the same terms.
suggested_refs: Art Institute of Chicago faculty records, 1906-1910
The Czech-language press of Chicago on Mucha's lectures

stops.name: New York, three murals on Irving Place
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1908
stops.campa: For the German Theatre on Irving Place he paints three large allegorical murals, Tragedy, Comedy, and Truth, and designs decoration for the house around them. It is theatre work again, twenty-eight years after the Vienna scenery shop, at the far side of an ocean, for an audience of German-speaking immigrants who go home from the theatre into an English-speaking city. It is the largest wall painting he has been given since the Bosnian pavilion of 1900, and the first since then on a subject nobody has asked him to make Slavic. The fee goes straight into the crossings and the sketchbooks.
suggested_refs: Irving Place Theatre (German Theatre), New York, and the fate of its Mucha murals

stops.name: New York, the birth of Jaroslava
stops.date_confidence: attested to 15 March 1909, New York
stops.campa: His daughter is born in New York on the fifteenth of March and they name her Jaroslava, a Slav name in Manhattan. She will grow up to restore her father's canvases and to fight for them. In the same months he is unrolling his sketches for the cycle in front of anyone in New York or Chicago who will sit through the explanation: twenty canvases, the history of the Slavs, painted at his own pace and given away at the end. The family is in America because the money for the cycle is in America. Nobody has yet said yes.
suggested_refs: Jaroslava Muchova, later conservator of the Slav Epic canvases

stops.name: Chicago, Charles Crane says yes
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia's article on Mucha dates Crane's agreement to February 1910 while the article on The Slav Epic dates it to 1909; the two are not reconciled here
stops.campa: Charles Richard Crane, heir to a Chicago plumbing-fittings fortune and a spender of it on Slavic and Middle Eastern causes, agrees to pay for the whole cycle: twenty monumental canvases on the history of the Slavs, painted over as many years as they take, and given free to the Czech nation at the end. No gallery commissions it and no state orders it. Twenty years of a painter's working life rest on one private agreement between a plumbing heir and a Moravian poster designer, made in February in Chicago. Mucha books his passage home.
suggested_refs: Charles R. Crane papers and his patronage of Slavic causes
The Slav Epic funding agreement

stops.name: Rosice, the first sketches
stops.date_confidence: the Mucha Foundation timeline places the first Slav Epic sketches at Rosice in 1909, in a gap between American trips
stops.campa: Back in Moravia between crossings, in the small town of Rosice on the road west of Brno, he opens the sketchbooks and lays out the cycle: the Slavs in their original homeland, the Slavonic liturgy, Jan Hus in the pulpit, the abolition of serfdom in Russia, twenty scenes ending in a nation still to come. He is fifty, and what remains of his working life is now accounted for. He works from the country rather than from books, walking out from Rosice to look at villages and at faces he can use.
stops.quote: I will be able to do something really good, not just for the art critic but for our Slav souls.
stops.quote_source: Mucha on returning to Prague and beginning the Slav Epic, quoted in Tomoko Sato, Mucha (Taschen, 2015), p. 73, as cited on the English Wikipedia article
suggested_refs: Preparatory sketchbooks for The Slav Epic, 1909-1912, Mucha Foundation

stops.name: Zbiroh, the hall with the high ceiling
stops.date_confidence: the Zbiroh studio tenancy runs 1910-1928; the coordinates are corrected to the castle west of the town centre, some two kilometres from the pin in the research pool
stops.campa: He rents rooms and a hall at Zbiroh, a castle in western Bohemia with a ceiling high enough to take a canvas six metres by eight, and rigs a scaffold that runs on rails so he can ride it across the picture. The largest canvases cannot be moved once stretched. He photographs models in costume in the courtyard, squares the compositions up from the prints, and paints in egg tempera so the surfaces stay matt and the canvases can be rolled. He will work in this building for eighteen years.
suggested_refs: Zbiroh Castle studio photographs, 1911-1928
Mucha's costumed model photographs for the Slav Epic

stops.name: Prague, the Lord Mayor's Hall
stops.date_confidence: begun 1910 and finished 1911; a claim in the research pool associating the room with a Josef Suk music room downstairs is unsupported and is dropped
stops.campa: The new Municipal House on the Republic Square gives him the Lord Mayor's Hall, and he takes no fee for it. On the ceiling he paints Slavic Concord; around the walls, the virtues of a nation that does not yet legally exist, each one wearing the face of a Czech hero, in a building standing inside an empire that reads the room correctly and dislikes it. He finishes in 1911. Prague's critics call the decoration Parisian and decorative and behind the times, and the city holds its ceremonies under it regardless.
suggested_refs: The Lord Mayor's Hall (Primatorsky sal), Obecni dum, Prague

stops.name: Mount Athos, inside the monasteries
stops.date_confidence: the Athos visit is attested as part of the research travel for the cycle, dated only loosely to about 1910-1913; the Croatian coast leg of the same research travel is reported without named ports and is not given its own stop here
stops.campa: For the cycle he goes to see the places themselves: Russia, Poland, the Balkans, and the Orthodox monasteries of Mount Athos on their peninsula in the Aegean, where no woman may set foot and the libraries hold Slavonic manuscripts a thousand years old. The canvas that comes out of it will show Athos as the Slavs' own Vatican, painted from inside the buildings rather than out of an engraving. He takes the boat, climbs the path, and draws the interiors, the lamps, the monks.
stops.quote: visiting the places he intended to depict in the cycle: Russia, Poland, and the Balkans, including the Orthodox Christian monasteries of Mount Athos
stops.quote_source: English Wikipedia, The Slav Epic, on Mucha's research travel
suggested_refs: Mount Athos monastic libraries and their Slavonic manuscripts
The Slav Epic canvas Mount Athos

stops.name: Moscow, the snow outside Saint Basil's
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1913 by the Mucha Foundation timeline and the Slav Epic literature
stops.campa: He travels to Russia and stands in the Red Square under the Kremlin wall, gathering material for the eastern canvases. What he wants from Moscow is the year 1861, the abolition of serfdom, and he paints it as a crowd standing in trodden snow outside Saint Basil's in the early morning, freed and not yet warm, the domes behind them in fog. He fills sketchbooks with faces, sledges, and the particular flat light coming off the snow. The Russia he is drawing from has four years left.
suggested_refs: The Slav Epic canvas The Abolition of Serfdom in Russia (1914)

stops.name: Prague, the birth of Jiri
stops.date_confidence: attested to 12 March 1915
stops.campa: His son is born in Prague on the twelfth of March, in the middle of the war, and is named Jiri. He will become a writer, will spend years in a communist labour camp, and will spend the rest of his life as keeper and biographer of his father's work, the reason much of it survives at all. Mucha is fifty-four. Austria is at war and the household is in Prague, while out in the Bohemian woods a Slav manifesto twenty canvases long is being painted inside the empire's own borders.
suggested_refs: Jiri Mucha, biographer of his father and custodian of the estate

stops.name: Prague, the banknotes of a new state
stops.date_confidence: the banknotes and first postage stamps, done without payment, are attested for 1918; the widely repeated claim that he also designed the state coat of arms is not attested in the sources consulted and is left out
stops.campa: Czechoslovakia is declared and the new state has no money of its own to print. Mucha designs the first banknotes and the first postage stamps for nothing, calling it a duty. He is fifty-eight, and Prague is at last a capital. Millions of people who will never stand in front of a poster of his will handle his drawing every day of their lives. On the hundred-koruna note he puts his portrait of Josephine Crane Bradley, the American patron's daughter, seated as Slavia with the wreath.
suggested_refs: The 1918 Czechoslovak 100-koruna note with the Slavia portrait
The first Czechoslovak postage stamps, Hradcany issue

stops.name: Prague, eleven canvases in the Klementinum
stops.date_confidence: attested; the 1919 Klementinum showing was of the first eleven canvases, not of the completed cycle as one line of the research pool implies
stops.campa: The first eleven canvases go on show in the Klementinum, unrolled and hung in the old Jesuit college for a country ten months old. Half the cycle is still unpainted. The crowds come, and so do the critics who find the whole enterprise a nineteenth-century history painting arriving a generation late, at the moment Prague is discovering cubism. The state the pictures were painted for is not certain it wants them. He goes back to Zbiroh and paints the remaining nine.
suggested_refs: The Klementinum exhibition of 1919, first public showing of The Slav Epic

stops.name: Prague, the cycle handed over
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1928, the tenth anniversary of independence; the final canvas, the Apotheosis of the Slavs, is dated 1926 and the American tour of the early 1920s is reported with attendance figures that are not independently verified
stops.campa: He finishes the twentieth canvas, the Apotheosis of the Slavs, in 1926 and formally gives the whole cycle to the city of Prague on the tenth anniversary of independence, on the condition that Prague build a hall to keep it in. The canvases had toured Chicago and New York earlier in the decade, drawing crowds reported in the tens of thousands a week. Charles Crane's money paid for every one of them. He is sixty-eight, and the city accepts the gift without building the hall.
suggested_refs: The deed of gift of The Slav Epic to the city of Prague, 1928
The Apotheosis of the Slavs (1926), final canvas of the cycle

stops.name: Prague Castle, the window at Saint Vitus
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1931
stops.campa: In the Archbishop's chapel of Saint Vitus, inside the castle, he designs a stained glass window for a cathedral finished six hundred years behind schedule, paid for by the Slavia insurance company whose advertisements he had also drawn. The subject is Cyril and Methodius, the brothers who brought the alphabet, the same pair he painted at twenty-six for a prairie parish in Dakota. This time the glass is set into the wall of the national cathedral and lit from behind.
suggested_refs: The Mucha window in the Archbishop's Chapel, St Vitus Cathedral, Prague, 1931

stops.name: Paris, the last exhibition
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1936
stops.campa: A hundred and thirty-nine works are hung at the Jeu de Paume, three of them canvases from the Slav Epic brought west from Prague, and Paris looks again at the man who papered its streets forty years earlier. He is seventy-six, and it is his last exhibition in the city. Paris made his name in a single morning of January 1895 and now receives him as a figure out of a closed period. Three enormous Slav canvases hang among the posters, making an argument the room is not following.
suggested_refs: Jeu de Paume, Paris, 1936 Mucha retrospective catalogue

stops.name: Prague, taken in for questioning
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1939, days after the German entry into Prague; the exact duration of the interrogation is not documented in the sources consulted
stops.campa: German troops enter Prague in March and Mucha is among the first people the Gestapo takes in. They have a file on him: Slav nationalism, Freemasonry, the twenty canvases, the banknotes of a state that has just ceased to exist. He is seventy-eight and is questioned and released. Waiting on his table at home is an unfinished triptych, The Age of Reason, Wisdom and Love, three panels arguing that reason, wisdom and love are the roads out of exactly what is now happening around him.
suggested_refs: The unfinished triptych The Age of Reason, Wisdom and Love, begun 1936

stops.name: Prague, ten days short of seventy-nine
stops.date_confidence: attested to 14 July 1939; the causal chain from interrogation to lung infection to pneumonia is the standard account rather than a medical record
stops.campa: He does not recover from the questioning. A lung infection takes hold and turns to pneumonia, and on the fourteenth of July, ten days short of his seventy-ninth birthday, Alphonse Mucha dies in Prague under German occupation. His daughter Jaroslava is thirty, his son Jiri twenty-four. The Slav Epic is already being taken down and wrapped against seizure. The country his last thirty years were painted for had been on the map for twenty years and has been off it for four months.
suggested_refs: The wrapping and hiding of The Slav Epic in 1939

stops.name: Vysehrad, the Slavin
stops.date_confidence: the burial at the Slavin is attested to July 1939; the sources consulted do not give the day, and the coordinates differ by some seventy metres between two entries of the research pool
stops.campa: He is buried at the Slavin, the common monument of the Vysehrad cemetery where the Czech nation keeps its writers, composers, and painters, on the rock above the Vltava. Public gatherings are forbidden under the occupation and a crowd of thousands comes anyway. The cycle he gave the city goes into hiding, surfaces in 1963 at a chateau in Moravsky Krumlov, and hangs there for half a century. Where it belongs, and who is to build the hall it was given on condition of, is still in front of the courts.
suggested_refs: The Slavin monument, Vysehrad Cemetery, Prague
The Moravsky Krumlov chateau display of The Slav Epic, 1963-2011
